features.name: Physics for loose objects
features.what: Avian becomes the one collision world: level parts and models get colliders, moving parts are kinematic, crates and barrels tumble, characters push and stand on them, blasts shove them.
chunks: Avian as the collision world: colliders for shapes and models (box, hull, convex pieces, exact for still things), still / moving / loose parts, a fixed time step with smoothing; Moves become moving bodies; the walker moves and slides through it

The walker on bevy_tnua (slopes, steps, moving platforms); a game's own character collides through Avian, and the old collision code retires (Last Ascent's mech moves when it is rebuilt as a character file)
Loose parts: mass, friction, sleeping; characters push and stand on them; impulses from blasts and the winch
features.note: Two collision worlds side by side (today's and Avian's) would need every moving part kept in step twice, so Avian replaces today's. Loose things need convex shapes (Avian builds them from the mesh); exact mesh colliders only for things that never move. avian3d 0.8 supports Bevy 0.20 and has f64 and enhanced-determinism options for big worlds and multiplayer. Part 1 (2026-11-15): avian3d 0.8 runs while playing on a fixed 60 Hz step, drawn smoothed between steps; each Solid part becomes a body (boxes as boxes; still shapes and models exact; loose ones a hull or convex pieces); a Physics setting (Still / Loose) on parts, shared by instances; Moves parts are moving bodies; the walker moves and slides through Avian and rides moving bodies; everything goes back when play stops. Test project: tests/physics. MCP: the Physics setting on add_part and change_part. Part 2 (2026-11-15): the walker is a bevy_tnua 0.33 character, a dynamic body floating 1.1 m up (it walks up steps of up to 0.45 m and slopes, and rides moving parts), grip and slippery feels (Slippery ground: slow to speed up and to stop); the old triangle collision (Play::world) is gone, and a game's own character collides through Avian (Play's doc comment). The user chose to rebuild Last Ascent's mech after Beverly is built instead of porting it now: notes for that are on The mech as a character file. Test project: tests/steps; the lift traces re-recorded for the new walker. MCP: get_play's velocity, ground and standing_on come from the walker's body. Part 3 (2026-11-16): the Physics setting is a switch (Still / Loose) with Weight (kg) and Grip under it; the walker (80 kg) shoves light loose parts and can't move heavy ones, and stands on them; resting loose parts fall asleep until touched (Avian's sleeping); Blast (an impulse outward, fading to the edge) and Pull (a winch: a force toward a point for a while) are messages for blasts and the grapple to send. Test project: tests/loose. MCP: blast and pull while testing, get_play's loose_parts (where, how far moved, asleep).

chunks: The design's parts from the SVG (cut by id, every shape, colour and coordinate kept) drawn in the editor, scaled to the window with only straight runs stretching; tabs and the Level menu (Physics, Cameras, Lighting topics); the three bottom panels and their drawers; Roboto lettering
True vector rendering: exact edges for the design's shapes and icons (no approximated fades), and no rasters anywhere in the GUI
features.note: Asked for by the user (2026-11-16), so built ahead of its place in the order. Part 1 built (2026-11-16): editor/assets/ui/editor.svg holds the user's design cut into parts by id; frame.rs reads it with usvg, tessellates each part with lyon and draws it as meshes, scaled to the window (two runs across and one down stretch, so curves, angles and the logo stay as drawn); the left drawer, inspector drawer and scene drawer slide up from below on the design's grip (drag for height). Part 2 built (2026-11-16): the user chose a small renderer of Beverly's own over a library. vector.rs draws each shape in egui's order (a paint callback); vector.wgsl covers each pixel by exactly how much of its square the shape covers, summed from the shape's own edges (a storage buffer), so curves, corners, thin strokes and holes match a browser's rendering of the SVG at any size. text.rs turns all of egui's text into vector letters at the places egui laid them out: each letter's outline (skrifa, the fonts egui was given) is tessellated once and kept on the GPU, and each frame only places it (position, size, turn, colour per letter, one draw per letter shape). egui still builds its letter atlas but nothing shows it. features.name: Brush tool
features.what: A round brush with size (a 10 cm dab to a 500 m forest), hardness (soft to hard, as in Photoshop), strength and spacing that paints onto terrain, water or any part: textures, heights or scattered props.
chunks: The brush on surfaces: the size and hardness rings drawn on the surface, Alt + right-drag to size and soften it, strokes painting material layers onto parts (soft edges blended in the shader), erase, undo

The brush as a shared tool: layers that other features fill (height on terrain, scatter sets, grass, water), size presets S / M / L / XL, strength as Add / Subtract (a little each pass) or Set (exactly this density), the rules any tool carries (slope limit, height band, keep clear of paths and water, spacing, which surfaces), Place (one item exactly) and Pick, brush presets, the MCP
features.note: Planned 2026-11-17. Round brush first; other brush types (textured tips, scatter tips, smudge) later. Stored as strokes (points, size, hardness, strength) and a seed, never as paint images: the shader blends layers from the strokes on parts and the terrain works them into its own description, so files stay small and every stroke can be undone or removed. Sizing as in Photoshop (user, 2026-11-17): [ and ] smaller / larger, Shift + [ and ] softer / harder, also Alt + right-drag; fly speed moved to Page Up / Page Down. MCP: paint_stroke (layer, points, size, hardness, strength). Shared kit (user, 2026-11-17): Place, Brush, Pen and Fill, the same keys in every tab; each tab says what they place (design.html, Brush, pen and fill). Keys (2026-11-17): V Place, B Brush, G Fill, I Pick, 1 to 4 brush presets; Alt erases with any tool; a plain right-click opens the menu or leaves the tool. Part 1 built (2026-11-18): B takes out the brush (Level tab); it paints the chosen material onto visible basic shapes in strokes kept on the part (Part::strokes: material, size, hardness, strength, points in the part's own frame in metres), one undo step each; Alt erases; [ ] size, Shift + [ ] hardness, Alt + right-drag sizes (across) and softens (up and down); the rings on the surface show the size and where the edge starts to fade (pink while erasing); Esc or a right-click puts it away. paint.rs draws each painted material as a see-through copy of the part whose shader (paint.wesl) works out the coverage from the strokes in order (a later stroke covers what is under it, erasing uncovers, a stroke counts once where its pieces overlap), in the editor and the game; textures repeat every 2 m. Its panel (Inspect) picks the material, Size, Hardness and Strength; clicking a material in Assets while the brush is out paints with it. Models aren't painted yet. Test project tests/brush. MCP: paint_stroke (part, material, points in the world, size, hardness, strength, erase, clear); get_part lists what is painted; the tool.brush action. Part 2 built (2026-11-18): the brush as the shared tool. Presets S, M, L and XL (keys 1 to 4 while it is out, a choice in its panel) each remember their size, hardness, strength and how they lay. Strength lays as Add (a little more each pass, covering other materials), Subtract (takes its own material away and leaves the others) or Set (exactly its strength, however often you go over it). Rules (Where it lands) go with every stroke: Slope (the steepest surface it lands on: Flat only paints tops, Any paints walls) and Only between heights are worked out in the shader where the stroke shows, so they hold wherever the part goes; Only on (a surface tag) picks which parts it paints. Keep clear of paths and water and spacing between items come with paths, water and scatter, which have nothing to keep clear of or space yet; the layers that grass, scatter, terrain heights and water fill are theirs to add (a stroke today lays a material). Pick (I): with the brush out, the material showing most under the pointer becomes the brush's; otherwise the part under the pointer becomes what Place puts down. Place (V) places the last thing placed or picked again (or opens the parts pop-up); while placing, the wheel turns it 15 degrees a notch about the surface and Shift + wheel sizes it, shown in its label. Test project tests/brush gained Subtract, Set and a block painted with rules. MCP: paint_stroke takes lays (add, subtract, set) and rules (slope, band, on); actions tool.place and tool.pick.

chunks: Shader assets: a settings header turned into sliders, hot reload, errors with the line, assigning a shader to a material; the paint layers move onto it

features.note: Part 1 built 2026-11-19 (shader assets): shader.rs. A shader is assets/shaders/NAME.wesl, a fragment shader for Bevy's standard material with header comment lines (@setting name "Label" 0..5 = 1 / colour / toggle, @see-through, @raster vertex_offset / alpha_mask) that Beverly turns into setting_NAME() functions (added after the code) and a values uniform; a material file gets shader and shader_values; the extension picks its fragment shader per material (specialize), so any shader works, not a fixed set. The file is read again about twice a second (hot reload); a header that doesn't parse keeps the last good shader and says which line in the island. Materials tab: a Shader choice and its settings as rows; Assets lists Shaders; MCP: get_shader, write_shader, change_material takes shader and shader_values, list_assets has shaders. Test project tests/shaders. Part 2 built 2026-11-19 (errors and raster hooks): code the graphics card refuses reaches the island and get_shader's problem with its line (the render side reads the pipeline cache), and a failing shader fails a scripted test; @raster vertex_offset / alpha_mask are functions the shader defines (vertex_offset(world, normal, uv), alpha_mask(world, uv)) that Beverly runs in its own vertex stage and in the depth and shadow passes, so shadows follow, with the part's bounds grown by the declared reach; @see-through makes an opaque material blend and alpha_mask makes it cut out; a shader with hooks keeps its fragment under @if(!PREPASS_PIPELINE) (tests/shaders lean.wesl). Not skinned, no motion vectors or deferred. Still to do: the paint layers moving onto it (they are already a Beverly shader; the move is for virtual geometry part 3, where the strokes have to be worked out in the material pass), and virtual geometry's use of the hooks. Planned 2026-11-18 (user: many shaders will be written, mostly through Claude; the pipeline must take any shader, not a fixed set). Every material goes through it, so virtual geometry can bin clusters by raster shader the way Nanite's programmable raster does.

features.name: Bezier pen tool
features.what: Click for corners, drag for smooth curves, close a loop on the first point; curves hug the surface under them and stay editable. Lays a strip, fills a shape, scatters along or inside it, or raises and carves.
chunks: The pen: click and drag points with Bezier handles, Alt breaks a handle, close on the first point, then move points and handles, insert and remove points; curves drawn on terrain, water and parts

What a pen shape does, with the brush’s layers: a strip along it (width, soft edges: a cobbled path), a fill inside it (feathered edge), scatter along or inside (Even: one every N metres facing along it; Scattered: a band thinning at its edges; Both sides), and height along or inside (ridges, beds, flat pads on terrain); shapes stay live, Turn into items makes placed items; the MCP
features.note: Part 1 built 2026-11-19 (the pen): P in the Level tab; click for a corner, drag for a smooth point, click the first point to close, Enter finishes; then drag points and handles, click the line to put a point on it, Alt + click a point (or Delete over it) removes it, Delete elsewhere removes the curve, click another curve to edit it, Alt while dragging breaks a handle; points snap to the grid like parts do and land on whatever surface is under the pointer. Curves live in the level file (curves: id, name, points with handle offsets, closed), one undo step per change; the code is curve.rs (the Bezier maths, tested) and editor/pen.rs. MCP: draw_shape (points as [x, y, z] or {at, handle_in, handle_out}, closed, shape to redraw, delete) and list_shapes (tests/mcp/check.py). Part 2, first slice built 2026-11-19 (stretches): each point carries how the line leaving it treats geometry, Ground (default), Over everything, Air or Fall, and the line seen is laid on what it meets (curve.rs laid, pen.rs surface; cached and relaid when the curve or any part changes): Ground takes the walkable surface (a top face, or a part tagged Ground or Water; never one tagged Paths ignore or an invisible collider) within half a metre up or two down from where it was, so it lies on a slab, passes under a prop or ceiling and bridges gaps; Over takes anything visible within 1.5 m up; Air ignores geometry; Fall leaves along its handle and ends where it lands. Ground stretches draw solid, Air and Fall dashed; a small button by the selected point switches its stretch (a new point goes on as the last one went); the Ground and Paths ignore tags are new surface tags; draw_shape points take stretch and list_shapes says it. Strips built 2026-11-19: the pen has a panel (Inspect while it is out: the curve's name, Paint a strip with a material, Width, Edge, Strength); a strip paints the laid line as brush strokes onto the part under each step of it (the part whose top face the point is on, so a prop the line passes through isn't painted and a stretch in the air paints nothing), kept in step with the curve: the strokes are the parts' own, marked with the curve (Stroke.curve), made again in place when the curve, its strip or the geometry changes and taken away with the strip or curve, in the same undo step; draw_shape takes strip {material, width, edge, strength} (null removes it) and list_shapes says it. Still to do: the path-wide default and Sag for air, the slope limit, fills, scatter and height along curves, and picking a curve without the pen. Decided with the user 2026-11-19: a path has two modes, Ground only (default: drapes onto the ground and ignores props, scatter and other paths) and Over everything (follows any geometry it meets); the surface each point was clicked on decides which level it follows, the path stays on that level between points, ground means surfaces within a slope limit and objects below step height, gaps are bridged, Water counts as ground; where two ground paths cross, the later one wins (order keys Ctrl+[ and ], Ctrl+Shift for ends, with a list in the Inspect panel, see the order note on the brush). Refined 2026-11-19 (user: a path crosses many surfaces; tags as well as rules; scatter on the ground, deep select for manual adjustment): the mode is per stretch (stored on a point, for the segment leaving it) with a path-wide default: Ground (walkable surfaces: ground, road, steps, interior floor; the path takes the walkable surface nearest in height to the previous sample within the step height, starting from the clicked level; ceilings and invisible colliders never count), Over everything, Air (ignores geometry; Sag for a rope) and Fall (leaves along its handle and drops until it hits a surface; a faucet stream is Fall then Ground). Tags: Ground forces a part to count, Paths ignore forces it out, Water counts. Precedence: the stretch's own behaviour, tags, the path's default, the slope and step rules. Scatter sits on the surface the path is following and never on other scatter; deep select (gesture to choose: Ctrl+click or double-click in; Alt is taken by the pen and brush) picks one scatter instance to nudge, delete or detach, kept as overrides by position along the curve (they can drift if the curve is reshaped a lot; Turn into items freezes everything). Confirmed by the user 2026-11-19: ground stretches draw as a solid line and air stretches dashed, with a small button on the selected point to switch its stretch behaviour; deep select is a double-click into the shape. Planned 2026-11-17. The one curve tool: the Paths tool draws its rails, patrols and roads with it. Stored as control points and handles. MCP: draw_shape (points, handles, closed, layer, width, feather). Idea (user, 2026-11-17): terrain features drawn with the pen, such as cliffs: a wedge along the curve with strong variation, and scatter (rocks) masking its seams. Live curves plus Turn into items (user, 2026-11-17). Characters tab later: hair, cloth strips and jewellery drawn with the pen, moving with physics. Keys (2026-11-17): P is the pen in the Level tab; points can also go in the air for camera and flying paths (the Paths overlay).

features.note: Scripted tests record today's mech before anything changes, so the port can be compared step by step. What to look for when converting it (Physics part 2, 2026-11-15): Beverly no longer hands a game's character the level's triangles (Play::world, with pieces() and offsets(), is gone), so Last Ascent's own editor and player stop building once they update past this; the user chose to rebuild the mech after Beverly is built, not to port it twice. Collision is now Avian's world while playing (physics.rs): each Solid part is a body tagged PartBody(id), still ones static, Moves ones kinematic (their LinearVelocity carries what stands on them), Loose ones dynamic, plus the ground at y = 0. The mech's own physics maps onto it: its sphere-against-triangles step becomes a body of its own (a bevy_tnua character like the walker in play.rs, or Avian's MoveAndSlide), its raycast (grapple, camera, ground) Avian's SpatialQuery::cast_ray, its ground_y (the legs' foot placement) a ray down, and riding moving parts comes free. Physics runs on the fixed 60 Hz step (single precision, Avian's Gravity 9.81 with GravityScale for heavier falls): the mech's movement moves from Update with a variable step to FixedUpdate, catching one-off keys every frame as play.rs does (Play::press), and still sets Play::feet for buttons. notes.title: Idles, barks and interaction
notes.text: Crowds look wrong when everyone plays the same idle: guides suggest 3–5 idle variations per character type and random offsets so footsteps don't sync. Fidgets (scratching, looking around) start after standing still a while. Head look-at is a cheap procedural layer, and hands reach handles with two-bone IK that blends in and out; holding is easy, the blend is the hard part.

notes.title: Driving
notes.text: Arcade handling starts simple and adds mechanics until it feels right: steering limited by speed (curbs understeer), the handbrake locks the rear wheels to start a drift, clean drifts refill boost, boost is spent on the way out. Simulation adds weight transfer and counter-steering; Beverly's vehicles start arcade with those as settings.
sources: Racing game approaches and trade-offs (Game Developer)
Need for Speed Heat handling model (EA)

notes.title: Flying
notes.text: Arcade flight keeps pitch, yaw and roll with automatic banking in turns, plus speed and lift limits. Manoeuvres become moves: aileron roll (a full roll), barrel roll (a roll with a pull, evasive), dive, loop, Immelmann (half loop and half roll: turn back, gain height), split-S (the reverse: turn back, gain speed), stall turn, boost.
sources: How to barrel roll (World of Warplanes)

notes.title: Moves and abilities
notes.text: Platformers hide forgiveness in jumping: coyote time (jump just after leaving an edge) and jump buffering. Air dashes usually reset on landing. Dodges pair a short invulnerability with a step; parries are timed blocks. Shooters add slide, wall-run and mantle; stealth adds crouch tiers, lean, cover and hiding in shadow.

notes.title: World sizes, terrain, caves
notes.text: Positions are 32-bit, so worlds past about 10 km jitter; the fix is a floating origin or camera-relative maths. Heightfields can't make overhangs; games add caves with sculpted volumes (smooth add / subtract shapes turned into meshes) or hand-made pieces, and build dungeons from modular kits, often laid out by a generator. Rooms joined by portals hide what can't be seen indoors; they don't suit open ground. Beverly's terrain is described by curves and strokes, not height images.
sources: Godot: double precision for large worlds

notes.title: Water
notes.text: Oceans layer a few Gerstner waves: stable and easy to tune. Rivers are paths with width, depth and flow speed per point; foam drifts with the flow. Waterfalls are usually custom pieces with mist and ripple rings where they land. Buoyancy samples the water height and pushes things up with drag. In Unreal, water fought with world streaming, so Beverly's water belongs to streaming regions from the start.

notes.title: Look: post-processing, styles, wind
notes.text: Bevy 0.20 already has depth of field, motion blur, bloom, chromatic aberration, vignette, lens distortion, colour grading, auto exposure, SSAO, screen-space reflections, volumetric fog, a physical sky, TAA / SMAA and GPU occlusion culling, so these are mostly editor work. Cel shading bands light into 2–5 steps; outlines are cheap shells (gaps on hard edges) or precise screen edge detection (costlier, noisier); games often mix them. One wind (direction, strength, gusts) feeds foliage sway in two layers, cloth, flags, particles and sails.
sources: Vegetation that reacts to the environment

notes.title: Multiplayer
notes.text: Shooters and most online games use an authoritative server: each player's own moves show at once and are corrected when the server answers. Rollback (every machine simulates and rewinds on a wrong guess) suits two-player fighting games and needs a deterministic game. Multiplayer touches characters, physics, scripting and saving, so if it's wanted it should be decided early, even if it's built late.

notes.title: Space and level edges
notes.text: Classic space games fly like aircraft; Newtonian flight keeps momentum, and Elite layers a switchable flight assist over it so ships stay controllable. For the edge of a level, games warn and count down (“return to the combat area”), push the player back, damage them in a hazard zone or wrap them around; developers report wrapping rarely feels good in 3D and round areas beat square ones.

notes.title: Risks found in the second pass
notes.text: Bevy releases every 3–4 months and each library has to catch up before Beverly can move, so Beverly stays pinned and upgrades on purpose (about a session each time). Physics: one collision world, not two. Animation: Prism has no skeletons yet, so pose and key comes to Beverly. Multiplayer: a fixed time step from the start. Effects: one particle system, Last Ascent's, and the Plume Editor's files as the effect format. Rasters: decals, reflections, foliage and terrain paint are kept as math, strokes or captured at load.
